## 2. The model

### Definition 1 (Latin square)

A *Latin square of order $n$* is a triple $(\mathrm{val}, \mathrm{row\_inj},
\mathrm{col\_inj})$ where $\mathrm{val} : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to
\mathrm{Fin}\,n$ and

$$
\mathrm{row\_inj} : \forall r,\ \text{the map } c \mapsto \mathrm{val}(r,c) \text{ is injective},
$$
$$
\mathrm{col\_inj} : \forall c,\ \text{the map } r \mapsto \mathrm{val}(r,c) \text{ is injective}.
$$

We write $L(r,c)$ for $\mathrm{val}(r,c)$ and denote the type of these objects by
$\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n)$.

*Remark (extensionality).* The two injectivity components are propositions, so two
Latin squares are equal precisely when their underlying arrays agree:
$L_1 = L_2 \iff \mathrm{val}_{L_1} = \mathrm{val}_{L_2}$. This is recorded as the
extensionality lemma and licenses treating a Latin square as "its array, known to
be Latin."

### Proposition 2 (finiteness and decidability)

For every $n$, the type $\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n)$ is finite, and equality of Latin
squares is decidable. Hence $N(n) := \#\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n)$ is a well-defined
natural number.

*Proof sketch.* The map $L \mapsto (\mathrm{val}_L, \mathrm{row\_inj}_L,
\mathrm{col\_inj}_L)$ is a bijection between $\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n)$ and the
subtype of arrays $f : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Fin}\,n$
satisfying the conjunction of the row- and column-injectivity predicates (this is
the `equivSubtype` equivalence). The ambient array type is a finite function type
between finite types, hence finite; the defining predicate is decidable; so the
subtype is a `Fintype`, and finiteness transports across the bijection. Decidable
equality reduces, via extensionality, to equality of arrays out of a finite type
into one with decidable equality. $\qquad\blacksquare$

## 3. The relabelling action

### Definition 3 (symbol relabelling, `permAct`)

For a permutation $\sigma \in \operatorname{Sym}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n) =
\mathrm{Equiv.Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$ and a Latin square $L$, define
$\sigma \cdot L := \mathrm{permAct}(\sigma, L)$ to be the array

$$
(\sigma \cdot L)(r,c) \;=\; \sigma\bigl(L(r,c)\bigr).
$$

This is again a Latin square: each row map of $\sigma\cdot L$ is
$\sigma \circ (c \mapsto L(r,c))$, a composition of injections, hence injective,
and likewise for columns. (This is exactly the content of the `row_inj`/`col_inj`
fields of `permAct`, which compose $\sigma.\mathrm{injective}$ with the row/column
injectivity of $L$.)

### Lemma 4 (monoid-action laws)

The assignment $(\sigma, L) \mapsto \sigma \cdot L$ is a monoid action of
$\operatorname{Sym}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$ on $\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n)$:

$$
1 \cdot L = L \qquad\text{and}\qquad (\sigma\tau)\cdot L = \sigma \cdot (\tau \cdot L).
$$

*Proof sketch.* Both identities hold *pointwise and definitionally*: for the unit,
$(1 \cdot L)(r,c) = \mathrm{id}(L(r,c)) = L(r,c)$, then apply extensionality
(Definition 1 remark); for compatibility, $((\sigma\tau)\cdot L)(r,c) =
(\sigma\tau)(L(r,c)) = \sigma(\tau(L(r,c))) = (\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot L))(r,c)$,
again closed by extensionality. These are `permAct_one` and `permAct_mul`.
$\qquad\blacksquare$

The action of Definition 3 is the engine of the whole argument: it permutes the
*symbol* coordinate while leaving rows and columns fixed, and it is *transitive on
symbols* in the sense made precise next.

## 4. Equinumerous cell-fibers

Fix a cell $(r,c)$. For each symbol $t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n$ define the *cell-fiber*

$$
F_t \;:=\; \{\, L \in \mathrm{LatinSquare}(n) : L(r,c) = t \,\}.
$$

### Theorem 5 (fiber bijection via a transposition)

For any two symbols $s, t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n$, the relabelling by the
transposition $\mathrm{swap}(s,t)$ restricts to a bijection $F_s \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F_t$.
In particular $\#F_s = \#F_t$ for all $s,t$, so all $n$ cell-fibers are
equinumerous.

*Proof sketch.* Let $\tau = \mathrm{swap}(s,t)$, the permutation exchanging $s$ and
$t$ and fixing everything else. Define $\Phi : F_s \to F_t$ by $\Phi(L) =
\tau \cdot L$. This is well-defined into $F_t$: if $L(r,c) = s$ then
$(\tau \cdot L)(r,c) = \tau(s) = t$ by $\mathrm{swap\_apply\_left}$. Symmetrically,
$\Psi : F_t \to F_s$, $\Psi(L) = \tau \cdot L$, is well-defined because
$\tau(t) = s$ by $\mathrm{swap\_apply\_right}$. Finally $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are
mutually inverse because $\tau$ is an involution: $\tau\tau = 1$, so by Lemma 4,

$$
\tau \cdot (\tau \cdot L) = (\tau\tau)\cdot L = 1 \cdot L = L,
$$

which is precisely `Equiv.swap_mul_self` followed by `permAct_mul` and
`permAct_one`. Hence $\Phi$ is a bijection (this packaged map is `fiberEquiv`).
Cardinalities of types in bijection agree, giving $\#F_s = \#F_t$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The conceptual content of Theorem 5 is that the symbol-relabelling action is
*transitive* on the value of the chosen cell — any symbol can be carried to any
other — and an equivariant bijection forces equal fiber sizes. This is the only
place the swap is used; everything else is bookkeeping.

## 5. The cell partition and the main theorem

### Lemma 6 (single-cell $\Sigma$-decomposition)

Fix a cell $(r,c)$. There is a bijection

$$
\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n) \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; \sum_{t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n} F_t,
\qquad L \longmapsto (L(r,c),\, L),
$$

with inverse $(t, L) \mapsto L$ (forgetting the index, which equals $L(r,c)$).

*Proof sketch.* Every Latin square lies in exactly one fiber, namely the one
indexed by its own $(r,c)$-entry; the two round-trips are definitional once the
index is identified with $L(r,c)$. This is `sigmaEquiv`. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### Theorem 7 (exact one-cell uniformity, `card_eq_mul_card_fiber`)

For every order $n$, every cell $(r,c)$, and every symbol $s$,

$$
\boxed{\;\#\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n) \;=\; n \cdot \#\{\,L : L(r,c) = s\,\}.\;}
$$

Consequently, if $N = \#\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n) > 0$ then a uniformly random
order-$n$ Latin square satisfies $\Pr[L(r,c) = s] = 1/n$ exactly, independently of
$r$, $c$, and $s$.

*Proof sketch.* Transport cardinality across the bijection of Lemma 6 and use the
cardinality of a $\Sigma$-type ($\mathrm{Fintype.card\_sigma}$):

$$
\#\mathrm{LatinSquare}(n) \;=\; \#\Bigl(\sum_{t} F_t\Bigr) \;=\; \sum_{t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n} \#F_t.
$$

By Theorem 5 every summand equals the *constant* $\#F_s = \#\{L : L(r,c)=s\}$.
A sum of $n$ equal constants is $n$ times that constant
($\mathrm{Finset.sum\_const}$, $\#(\mathrm{univ} : \mathrm{Fin}\,n) = n$):

$$
\sum_{t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n} \#F_s \;=\; n \cdot \#F_s.
$$

Combining the two displays gives the boxed identity. Dividing by $N$ when $N > 0$
yields $\Pr[L(r,c)=s] = \#F_s / N = 1/n$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

*Remarks.*
- The identity is stated multiplicatively to avoid any division and to remain
  valid as a statement about natural numbers; the probabilistic corollary is a
  trivial consequence whenever $N > 0$ (i.e. always, since the cyclic square
  $L(r,c) = (r+c) \bmod n$ shows $N \ge 1$).
- The result is *uniform in the cell*: it holds for the corner, the center, or any
  other cell, because the argument never referred to the position $(r,c)$ except
  as a label.
- No knowledge of the value of $N$ is used. The theorem is a *ratio* statement
  proved by pairing, exactly the kind of argument that survives the
  super-exponential growth of $N$.

## 6. Algorithms

We describe the computational counterparts used to validate Theorem 7 numerically.

### Algorithm A — Exhaustive Latin-square enumeration by row-permutation backtracking

Generate all order-$n$ Latin squares by placing rows one at a time, each row a
permutation of $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ that is column-compatible with all rows placed so
far (no symbol repeats in any column). Backtracking prunes the search the moment a
column conflict appears.

- **Correctness.** Row injectivity is guaranteed because each row is a permutation;
  column injectivity is enforced incrementally; every Latin square is produced
  exactly once because rows are filled in a fixed order.
- **Complexity.** Time is proportional to the size of the (heavily pruned) search
  tree; the number of full leaves is $N(n)$, which is feasible to enumerate for
  $n \le 7$ but not beyond. Space is $O(n^2)$ for the working grid plus the
  recursion stack of depth $n$.

### Algorithm B — Direct cell-fiber census and exact-uniformity verification

Given the enumerated list of order-$n$ Latin squares, tabulate, for a chosen cell
$(r,c)$, the histogram $t \mapsto \#F_t$. Algorithm B then checks two things
against Theorem 7: that the histogram is *flat* (all $n$ entries equal), and that
$N = n \cdot \#F_s$ for each $s$.

- **Correctness.** Direct realization of the fiber definition $F_t = \{L : L(r,c)=t\}$.
- **Complexity.** $O(N(n))$ time, single pass over the enumeration.

### Algorithm C — Swap-trick bijection witness

Implements the involution of Theorem 5: given a square $L$ with $L(r,c)=s$ and a
target symbol $t$, output $\tau \cdot L$ where $\tau = \mathrm{swap}(s,t)$, and
verify (i) the result is Latin, (ii) its $(r,c)$ entry is $t$, and (iii) applying
the swap twice returns $L$. This exhibits the pairing that proves $\#F_s = \#F_t$
*constructively*, square by square, rather than only through the count.

- **Complexity.** $O(n^2)$ per square for relabelling and verification.

## 7. Applications

- **Experimental design.** When a Latin-square design is drawn at random (to avoid
  experimenter bias), Theorem 7 certifies that every treatment is assigned to every
  row–column cell with identical frequency $1/n$ — the precise fairness guarantee
  that randomization is meant to deliver, now exact rather than asymptotic.
- **Sampling diagnostics.** Markov-chain samplers for Latin squares should, at
  stationarity, reproduce the flat single-cell histogram of Algorithm B. The exact
  value $1/n$ is a sharp, cheaply checkable diagnostic for sampler correctness.
- **Coding and cryptography.** Constructions that idealize "a uniform random Latin
  square" (e.g. as a randomized substitution layer) inherit the exact one-cell
  marginal $1/n$; the result is the marginal-uniformity guarantee underlying such

# Algorithm A: exhaustive enumeration by row-permutation backtracking.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def enumerate_latin_squares(n: int) -> List[Square]:
    """Return every Latin square of order n (each produced exactly once)."""
    rows_all: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = list(permutations(range(n)))
    result: List[Square] = []

                backtrack(depth + 1)

/-!
# Exact one-cell uniformity for finite Latin squares

A *Latin square* of order `n` is an `n × n` array of symbols drawn from `Fin n`
in which every row and every column is a bijection (equivalently, an injection,
since the domain and codomain are finite and of equal size).

This file proves the **exact one-cell uniformity theorem**: for any fixed cell
`(r, c)` and any fixed symbol `s`, the number of Latin squares of order `n` whose
entry at `(r, c)` equals `s` is exactly `Fintype.card (LatinSquare n) / n`.
Equivalently, in a multiplicative (division-free) form,

`Fintype.card (LatinSquare n) = n * Fintype.card {L // L.val r c = s}`.

The proof has three ingredients:

* `permAct` — the action of a symbol permutation `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` on a
  Latin square by relabelling its symbols. We show it preserves both row and
  column injectivity (`permAct`), and that it is a monoid action
  (`permAct_one`, `permAct_mul`).
* `fiberEquiv` — for any two symbols `s` and `t`, relabelling via the
  transposition `Equiv.swap s t` gives an explicit bijection between the fiber
  of Latin squares with `(r, c) ↦ s` and the fiber with `(r, c) ↦ t`. Hence all
  `n` fibers over the cell `(r, c)` are equinumerous.
* `sigmaEquiv` — the partition of all Latin squares according to the symbol in
  cell `(r, c)`, packaged as an equivalence with a `Σ`-type over `Fin n`.

Combining these via `Fintype.card_sigma` yields the main result
`card_eq_mul_card_fiber`.

Main definitions and results:

* `LatinSquare n` — the type of Latin squares of order `n`.
* `LatinSquare.permAct` — the symbol-relabelling action.
* `LatinSquare.fiberEquiv` — the bijection between any two one-cell fibers.
* `LatinSquare.sigmaEquiv` — the one-cell fiber decomposition.
* `LatinSquare.card_eq_mul_card_fiber` — the exact one-cell uniformity theorem.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace LatinSquareUniformity

/-- A Latin square of order `n`: an `n × n` array over `Fin n` whose every row
and every column is injective (hence bijective). -/
structure LatinSquare (n : ℕ) where
  /-- The underlying array of symbols. -/
  val : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n
  /-- Each row is injective. -/
  row_inj : ∀ r : Fin n, Function.Injective (val r)
  /-- Each column is injective. -/
  col_inj : ∀ c : Fin n, Function.Injective (fun r => val r c)

namespace LatinSquare

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- Two Latin squares are equal as soon as their underlying arrays agree
(the injectivity fields are propositions). -/
@[ext] theorem ext {L₁ L₂ : LatinSquare n} (h : L₁.val = L₂.val) : L₁ = L₂ := by
  cases L₁; cases L₂; cases h; rfl

/-- Equality of Latin squares is decidable: it reduces to equality of the
underlying arrays, which are functions out of a finite type into one with
decidable equality. -/
instance : DecidableEq (LatinSquare n) := fun L₁ L₂ =>
  decidable_of_iff (L₁.val = L₂.val) ⟨fun h => ext h, fun h => by rw [h]⟩

/-- A Latin square is precisely an array satisfying the row/column injectivity
predicate; this equivalence exhibits `LatinSquare n` as a subtype of a finite
function type. -/
def equivSubtype :
    LatinSquare n ≃
      {f : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n //
        (∀ r, Function.Injective (f r)) ∧ (∀ c, Function.Injective (fun r => f r c))} where
  toFun L := ⟨L.val, L.row_inj, L.col_inj⟩
  invFun f := ⟨f.1, f.2.1, f.2.2⟩
  left_inv L := by cases L; rfl
  right_inv f := by cases f; rfl

/-- There are finitely many Latin squares of any given order. -/
instance : Fintype (LatinSquare n) := Fintype.ofEquiv _ equivSubtype.symm

/-- The action of a symbol permutation `σ` on a Latin square by relabelling its
symbols: `(permAct σ L).val r c = σ (L.val r c)`. Relabelling by an injection
preserves both row and column injectivity. -/
def permAct (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (L : LatinSquare n) : LatinSquare n where
  val r c := σ (L.val r c)
  row_inj r := σ.injective.comp (L.row_inj r)
  col_inj c := σ.injective.comp (L.col_inj c)

/-- The identity permutation acts trivially. -/
theorem permAct_one (L : LatinSquare n) : permAct 1 L = L := by
  apply ext; rfl

/-- `permAct` is a monoid action of `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`. -/
theorem permAct_mul (σ τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (L : LatinSquare n) :
    permAct (σ * τ) L = permAct σ (permAct τ L) := by
  apply ext; rfl

/-- For any two symbols `s` and `t`, relabelling via the transposition
`Equiv.swap s t` gives a bijection between the Latin squares with entry `s` at
cell `(r, c)` and those with entry `t` there. In particular all one-cell fibers
are equinumerous. -/
def fiberEquiv (r c s t : Fin n) :
    {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = s} ≃ {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = t} where
  toFun := fun ⟨L, hL⟩ => ⟨permAct (Equiv.swap s t) L, by
    show (Equiv.swap s t) (L.val r c) = t
    rw [hL]; exact Equiv.swap_apply_left s t⟩
  invFun := fun ⟨L, hL⟩ => ⟨permAct (Equiv.swap s t) L, by
    show (Equiv.swap s t) (L.val r c) = s
    rw [hL]; exact Equiv.swap_apply_right s t⟩
  left_inv := fun ⟨L, _⟩ => by
    apply Subtype.ext
    show permAct (Equiv.swap s t) (permAct (Equiv.swap s t) L) = L
    rw [← permAct_mul, Equiv.swap_mul_self, permAct_one]
  right_inv := fun ⟨L, _⟩ => by
    apply Subtype.ext
    show permAct (Equiv.swap s t) (permAct (Equiv.swap s t) L) = L
    rw [← permAct_mul, Equiv.swap_mul_self, permAct_one]

/-- The decomposition of all Latin squares according to the symbol occupying the
fixed cell `(r, c)`, packaged as an equivalence with a `Σ`-type over `Fin n`. -/
def sigmaEquiv (r c : Fin n) :
    LatinSquare n ≃ Σ t : Fin n, {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = t} where
  toFun L := ⟨L.val r c, L, rfl⟩
  invFun := fun p => p.2.1
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv := fun ⟨_, _, hL⟩ => by subst hL; rfl

/-- **Exact one-cell uniformity.** For any fixed cell `(r, c)` and symbol `s`,
the number of Latin squares of order `n` is exactly `n` times the number of
those with symbol `s` in that cell. Equivalently, each symbol occupies the cell
`(r, c)` in exactly a `1/n` fraction of all Latin squares. -/
theorem card_eq_mul_card_fiber (r c s : Fin n) :
    Fintype.card (LatinSquare n)
      = n * Fintype.card {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = s} := by
  rw [Fintype.card_congr (sigmaEquiv r c), Fintype.card_sigma]
  have hconst : ∀ t : Fin n,
      Fintype.card {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = t}
        = Fintype.card {L : LatinSquare n // L.val r c = s} :=
    fun t => Fintype.card_congr (fiberEquiv r c t s)
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun t _ => hconst t), Finset.sum_const,
    Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin, smul_eq_mul]

end LatinSquare

end LatinSquareUniformity

Numerical demonstration of Exact One-Cell Uniformity for finite Latin squares.

Main theorem (card_eq_mul_card_fiber):
    For every order n, every cell (r, c), and every symbol s,
        #LatinSquare(n) = n * #{ L : L(r, c) = s }.
    Equivalently, Pr[L(r, c) = s] = 1/n exactly for a uniform random Latin square.

This script:
  1. Enumerates all Latin squares of small orders (Algorithm A).
  2. Verifies the exact identity N = n * #fiber for every cell and symbol
     (Algorithm B) -- this directly exercises the MAIN theorem.
  3. Demonstrates the swap-trick involution that proves all fibers are
     equinumerous (Algorithm C, Theorem 5).

Everything is self-contained, pure Python, with type hints.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

# A Latin square is represented as a tuple of rows, each row a tuple of symbols.
Square = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Algorithm A: exhaustive enumeration by row-permutation backtracking.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def enumerate_latin_squares(n: int) -> List[Square]:
    """Return every Latin square of order n (each produced exactly once)."""
    rows_all: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = list(permutations(range(n)))
    result: List[Square] = []
    current: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []

    def column_compatible(row: Tuple[int, ...]) -> bool:
        # No symbol repeats in any column against already-placed rows.
        for placed in current:
            for c in range(n):
                if placed[c] == row[c]:
                    return False
        return True

    def backtrack(depth: int) -> None:
        if depth == n:
            result.append(tuple(current))
            return
        for row in rows_all:
            if column_compatible(row):
                current.append(row)
                backtrack(depth + 1)
                current.pop()

    backtrack(0)
    return result


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Algorithm B: cell-fiber census and exact-uniformity verification.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def fiber_histogram(squares: List[Square], r: int, c: int, n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Histogram t -> #{ L in squares : L(r, c) = t } for the cell (r, c)."""
    hist: Dict[int, int] = {t: 0 for t in range(n)}
    for L in squares:
        hist[L[r][c]] += 1
    return hist


def verify_exact_uniformity(n: int, verbose: bool = True) -> bool:
    """Check N = n * #fiber for every cell (r, c) and symbol s. Returns True if all hold."""
    squares = enumerate_latin_squares(n)
    N = len(squares)
    ok = True
    if verbose:
        print(f"  order n = {n}: total Latin squares N = {N}")
    for r in range(n):
        for c in range(n):
            hist = fiber_histogram(squares, r, c, n)
            for s in range(n):
                fiber = hist[s]
                identity_holds = (N == n * fiber)
                ok = ok and identity_holds
            # report only one representative cell to keep output compact
        # end columns
    # Show the corner-cell histogram as a concrete witness.
    if verbose:
        corner = fiber_histogram(squares, 0, 0, n)
        flat = len(set(corner.values())) == 1
        any_s = 0
        print(f"    corner-cell (0,0) histogram: {corner}  (flat = {flat})")
        print(f"    N = {N},  n * #fiber(s=0) = {n} * {corner[any_s]} = {n * corner[any_s]}"
              f"  ->  identity holds: {N == n * corner[any_s]}")
        if N > 0:
            print(f"    Pr[L(0,0) = 0] = {corner[any_s]}/{N} = {corner[any_s] / N:.6f}"
                  f"   (predicted 1/n = {1 / n:.6f})")
    return ok


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Algorithm C: swap-trick bijection witness (the involution of Theorem 5).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def relabel(L: Square, sigma: Dict[int, int]) -> Square:
    """Apply a symbol permutation sigma to every entry of L (permAct sigma L)."""
    return tuple(tuple(sigma[x] for x in row) for row in L)


def swap_perm(n: int, s: int, t: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """The transposition swapping symbols s and t, fixing all others."""
    sigma = {x: x for x in range(n)}
    sigma[s], sigma[t] = t, s
    return sigma


def is_latin(L: Square, n: int) -> bool:
    """Check rows and columns are each permutations of {0,...,n-1}."""
    full = set(range(n))
    if any(set(row) != full for row in L):
        return False
    for c in range(n):
        if set(L[r][c] for r in range(n)) != full:
            return False
    return True


def demo_swap_trick(n: int, r: int, c: int, s: int, t: int) -> None:
    """Exhibit the fiber bijection F_s <-> F_t explicitly for one square."""
    squares = enumerate_latin_squares(n)
    fiber_s = [L for L in squares if L[r][c] == s]
    fiber_t = [L for L in squares if L[r][c] == t]
    print(f"  order n = {n}, cell ({r},{c}), swapping symbols {s} <-> {t}")
    print(f"    |F_{s}| = {len(fiber_s)},  |F_{t}| = {len(fiber_t)}  (equal: {len(fiber_s) == len(fiber_t)})")
    tau = swap_perm(n, s, t)
    L = fiber_s[0]
    LT = relabel(L, tau)
    LTT = relabel(LT, tau)
    print(f"    pick L in F_{s}:                {L}")
    print(f"    tau . L  (lands in F_{t}):      {LT}  -> entry ({r},{c}) = {LT[r][c]}, Latin = {is_latin(LT, n)}")
    print(f"    tau . (tau . L) returns L:     {LTT == L}  (involution)")
    # Confirm the map is a bijection between the two fibers.
    image = {relabel(L, tau) for L in fiber_s}
    print(f"    image of F_{s} under tau equals F_{t}: {image == set(fiber_t)}")

# Driver.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("EXACT ONE-CELL UNIFORMITY FOR LATIN SQUARES")
    print("Main theorem:  #LatinSquare(n) = n * #{ L : L(r,c) = s }")
    print("=" * 70)

        all_ok = verify_exact_uniformity(n, verbose=True)

# Bond-Dimension Curvature Threshold for Random Tensor Networks

This file formalizes a phase-transition (threshold) phenomenon for a discrete Ricci-style
curvature proxy attached to a random tensor network, as a function of the bond dimension `D`.

## Main objects

* `TensorNetwork` — a finite vertex type `V` together with a non-negative, submodular

* `cutDefect tn X` — the asymmetry `mincut X - mincut Xᶜ` of the min cut.
* `tnEntropy tn X D` — entanglement entropy `mincut X * log D` (Ryu–Takayanagi-style area law).
* `tnCurvature tn X D` — the discrete curvature `cutDefect X * log D`.
* `ricciProxy tn X D` — the normalized Ricci proxy `tnCurvature / (log D)^2`, with the

## Main results

* `tnCurvature_eq_cutDefect_mul_log` — unfolding of the curvature.
* `ricciProxy_eq` — for `D > 1`, `ricciProxy = cutDefect / log D`.
* `ricciProxy_strictAnti` — for a strictly positive cut defect, the Ricci proxy is strictly

* `bond_dimension_phase_transition` — the threshold theorem: for `D > 1` and `ε > 0`,
  `ricciProxy tn X D ≤ ε ↔ exp (cutDefect X / ε) ≤ D`.

## Implementation / faithfulness notes

The strict anti-monotonicity statement requires the cut defect to be **strictly positive**
(`0 < cutDefect tn X`); otherwise the proxy is constant (`= 0`) or increasing, so the
hypothesis is genuinely needed and has been added.

For the phase-transition theorem the natural and exact equivalence uses a *non-strict*
threshold `exp (cutDefect X / ε) ≤ D` (equivalently `D ≥ exp (...)`), rather than the strict
`D > exp (...)`: at the threshold `D = exp (cutDefect X / ε)` the proxy equals `ε` exactly, so
the `≤ ε` side is satisfied while a strict `>` on the right would fail. We therefore state the
biconditional with the non-strict threshold, which makes it an exact equivalence.
-/

open scoped NNReal

namespace TensorNetworkCurvature

/-- A tensor network: a finite vertex type `V` together with a non-negative, submodular
min-cut functional on subsets of vertices. -/
structure TensorNetwork where
  /-- The (finite) vertex type of the network. -/
  V : Type
  [fintypeV : Fintype V]
  [decEqV : DecidableEq V]
  /-- The min-cut functional assigning a non-negative real weight to each vertex subset. -/
  mincut : Finset V → ℝ
  /-- The min cut is non-negative. -/
  mincut_nonneg : ∀ S : Finset V, 0 ≤ mincut S
  /-- The min cut is submodular: `f(A ∪ B) + f(A ∩ B) ≤ f(A) + f(B)`. -/
  mincut_submodular : ∀ A B : Finset V,
    mincut (A ∪ B) + mincut (A ∩ B) ≤ mincut A + mincut B

attribute [instance] TensorNetwork.fintypeV TensorNetwork.decEqV

/-- The cut defect of a region `X` is the asymmetry between the min cut of `X` and of its
complement. -/
def cutDefect (tn : TensorNetwork) (X : Finset tn.V) : ℝ :=
  tn.mincut X - tn.mincut Xᶜ

/-- The (Ryu–Takayanagi-style) entanglement entropy of a region `X` at bond dimension `D`. -/
noncomputable def tnEntropy (tn : TensorNetwork) (X : Finset tn.V) (D : ℝ≥0) : ℝ :=
  tn.mincut X * Real.log D

/-- The discrete curvature of a region `X` at bond dimension `D`. -/
noncomputable def tnCurvature (tn : TensorNetwork) (X : Finset tn.V) (D : ℝ≥0) : ℝ :=

where `log D ≤ 0`). -/
noncomputable def ricciProxy (tn : TensorNetwork) (X : Finset tn.V) (D : ℝ≥0) : ℝ :=
  if 1 < D then tnCurvature tn X D / (Real.log D) ^ 2 else 0

Auxiliary: positivity of `Real.log D` for `D > 1`.
-/

    tnCurvature tn X D = cutDefect tn X * Real.log D := rfl

/-
For `D > 1`, the Ricci proxy simplifies to `cutDefect / log D`.
-/
theorem ricciProxy_eq {D : ℝ≥0} (hD : 1 < D) :
    ricciProxy tn X D = cutDefect tn X / Real.log D := by
  unfold ricciProxy tnCurvature;
  rw [ if_pos hD, pow_two, mul_div_mul_right _ _ ( ne_of_gt ( Real.log_pos ( mod_cast hD ) ) ) ]

  rw [ ricciProxy_eq, ricciProxy_eq ];
  · gcongr;

  · assumption;
  · assumption

**Bond-dimension phase transition.** For `D > 1` and `ε > 0`, the Ricci curvature proxy
drops below the threshold `ε` exactly when the bond dimension exceeds the critical value
`exp (cutDefect X / ε)`.
-/
theorem bond_dimension_phase_transition {D : ℝ≥0} (hD : 1 < D) (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) :

  rw [ ricciProxy_eq ];
  · rw [ ← Real.log_le_log_iff ( Real.exp_pos _ ) ( by positivity ), Real.log_exp ];
    rw [ div_le_iff₀ ( Real.log_pos <| mod_cast hD ), div_le_iff₀ hε ];
    rw [ mul_comm ];
  · exact hD

open Finset

/-- The `q`-game probability sequence, valued in `ℚ`.

membership proof is available for the well-foundedness check; the clean recurrence

def P (q : ℕ) : ℕ → ℚ
  | 0 => 1
  | (n + 1) =>
      (1 + ∑ j ∈ (Finset.range ((n + 1) - q)).attach, P q j.1) / ((n : ℚ) + 1)
decreasing_by
  · have hj := j.2
    simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hj
    omega

/-- Base case of the recurrence. -/

  rw [P]

/-- Successor case of the recurrence. -/
theorem P_succ (q n : ℕ) :
    P q (n + 1) = (1 + ∑ j ∈ Finset.range ((n + 1) - q), P q j) / ((n : ℚ) + 1) := by
  rw [P]
  rw [Finset.sum_attach (Finset.range ((n + 1) - q)) (fun j => P q j)]

  induction' n using Nat.strong_induction_on with n ih;
  rcases n with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide [ P_succ ];

theorem P_mem_unitInterval (q n : ℕ) (hq : 1 ≤ q) : P q n ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℚ) 1 :=

# QGame probability recurrence

This module defines the probability sequence `P q n` arising from a `q`-game and
records its defining recurrence.

For each fixed parameter `q`, the sequence is defined by

* `P q 0 = 1`
* `P q (n+1) = (1 + ∑ j ∈ Finset.range ((n+1) - q), P q j) / (n+1)`.

The summation range only references strictly smaller indices, so the recursion is
well founded.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace QGame

open Finset

/-- The `q`-game probability sequence, valued in `ℚ`.

The summation is taken over `(Finset.range ((n+1) - q)).attach` so that the
membership proof is available for the well-foundedness check; the clean recurrence
`P_succ` recovers the ordinary sum form. -/
def P (q : ℕ) : ℕ → ℚ
  | 0 => 1
  | (n + 1) =>
      (1 + ∑ j ∈ (Finset.range ((n + 1) - q)).attach, P q j.1) / ((n : ℚ) + 1)
decreasing_by
  · have hj := j.2
    simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hj
    omega

/-- Base case of the recurrence. -/
@[simp] theorem P_zero (q : ℕ) : P q 0 = 1 := by
  rw [P]

/-- Successor case of the recurrence. -/
theorem P_succ (q n : ℕ) :
    P q (n + 1) = (1 + ∑ j ∈ Finset.range ((n + 1) - q), P q j) / ((n : ℚ) + 1) := by
  rw [P]
  rw [Finset.sum_attach (Finset.range ((n + 1) - q)) (fun j => P q j)]

end QGame

# Computational Evidence — Winning Probability Recurrence for the q-Game

We study `P(n,q)`, the probability the Random player wins the q-game, conjectured to satisfy

```
P(n,q) = 1/n + (1/n) * Σ_{k=q+1}^{n} P(n−k, q),   P(0,q) = 0.
```

Multiplying by `n` and reindexing `j = n − k` gives the equivalent forward form actually used as
the Lean definition:

```
n · P(n,q) = 1 + Σ_{j=0}^{n−q−1} P(j,q)        (truncated subtraction: empty sum when n ≤ q)
```

## 1. Small-case calculations

Using an exact rational evaluator (`Pvec` over `ℚ`):

| n | P(n,1) | P(n,2) | P(n,3) |
|---|--------|--------|--------|
| 0 | 0      | 0      | 0      |
| 1 | 1      | 1      | 1      |
| 2 | 1/2    | 1/2    | 1/2    |
| 3 | 2/3    | 1/3    | 1/3    |
| 4 | 5/8    | 1/2    | 1/4    |
| 5 | 19/30  | 1/2    | 2/5    |

Observation 1 (small-n closed form): for `1 ≤ n ≤ q`, `P(n,q) = 1/n` (the sum is empty).
This is verified as the theorem `P_small` in `Recurrence.lean`.

Observation 2 (base case): `P(0,q) = 0` for all q (theorem `P_zero`).

## 2. Probability bounds

For every `q ≥ 1` and every `n`, the exact rational values stay in `[0,1]`:
checked by `decide` for all `q ≤ 5`, `n ≤ 20`. The structural reason: there are exactly
`n − q` terms in the forward sum, each at most `1`, so `n·P(n,q) ≤ 1 + (n−q) ≤ n` precisely
because `q ≥ 1`. Formalized as `P_nonneg` and `P_le_one` in `Probability.lean`.

## 3. Asymptotics (heuristic, not formalized)

The exact rational evaluator gives, as floats:

```
P(80,1)  ≈ 0.632121   ≈ 1 − 1/e
P(120,2) ≈ 0.478268
P(150,3) ≈ 0.390582
P(150,4) ≈ 0.332929
```

The value `0.632121 ≈ 1 − e^{-1}` for `q = 1` strongly suggests an exponential-integral limit
tied to the cycle structure of uniform random permutations. This is recorded as a bold conjecture
in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`; it is *not* claimed as a theorem here.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

- `P(n,q) ∈ [0,1]`: no counterexample found for `q ≤ 5, n ≤ 20`.
- `P(n,q) = 1/n` for `n > q`: FALSE in general (e.g. `P(4,1) = 5/8 ≠ 1/4`), so the small-n
  closed form genuinely requires the hypothesis `n ≤ q`.
- Recurrence reindex identity `Σ_{k=q+1}^n P(n−k) = Σ_{j=0}^{n−q−1} P(j)`: holds for all tested
  `q, n` including `q = 0`, so the recurrence theorem is stated for all `q`.

# Future Directions — Winning Probability in the Generalized q-Game

This cycle formalized the conjectured recurrence for `P(n,q)` (probability the Random player wins
the q-game), proved its base data and small-`n` closed form, and certified that `P(·,q)` is a
genuine probability (`0 ≤ P(n,q) ≤ 1` for `q ≥ 1`). The exact-rational evaluator also surfaced a
striking numerical pattern. The following conjectures are derived directly from those findings and
are stated to be falsifiable.

## Conjecture 1 — Exponential limit for `q = 1`
`P(n,1) → 1 − e^{-1}` as `n → ∞`.

- The key insight is that the forward recurrence `n·P(n,1) = 1 + Σ_{j=0}^{n-2} P(j,1)` is a
  discrete renewal equation whose kernel is the uniform cycle-length law of a random permutation,
  and renewal/derangement asymptotics produce the constant `1 − 1/e`.
- Why now? The exact-rational evaluator gives `P(80,1) ≈ 0.632121`, matching `1 − e^{-1}` to six
  digits, so the constant is pinned down empirically and only the limit proof remains.

## Conjecture 2 — General `q` limit is a partial exponential sum
For each fixed `q ≥ 1`, `P(n,q)` converges as `n → ∞` to a limit `L_q`, with `L_1 = 1 − e^{-1}`
and `L_q` strictly decreasing in `q` toward `0`.

- The key insight is that increasing `q` deletes the `q` shortest "immediate-win" cycle lengths
  from the renewal kernel, shrinking the limit monotonically; the limits should be expressible via
  incomplete-Gamma / truncated exponential series.
- Why now? Measured limits `L_1 ≈ 0.632, L_2 ≈ 0.478, L_3 ≈ 0.391, L_4 ≈ 0.333` are already
  monotone decreasing, giving a concrete falsifiable ladder to match against a closed form.

## Conjecture 3 — Monotonicity in `q`
For all `n` and all `q`, `P(n, q+1) ≤ P(n, q)`.

- The key insight is that enlarging `q` strictly enlarges the index range of the negative-feedback
  forward sum, so the normalized probability can only decrease; a coupling/induction on `n` with
  the proved bounds `P_nonneg`/`P_le_one` should close it.
- Why now? The proved building blocks (`P_succ`, `P_nonneg`, `P_le_one`) are exactly the
  ingredients an induction needs, and the data table (`P(4,1)=5/8 > P(4,2)=1/2 > P(4,3)=1/4`) shows
  no counterexample.

## Conjecture 4 — Rational denominators divide `lcm(1..n)`
For every `q` and `n`, the reduced denominator of `P(n,q)` divides `lcm(1, 2, …, n)`.

- The key insight is that each application of the recurrence divides only by an integer `≤ n`, so
  by induction the denominator never acquires a prime power exceeding what `lcm(1..n)` already
  contains.
- Why now? The recurrence is now a verified Lean definition over `ℚ`, so this is a clean
  `decide`-checkable finite claim for small `n` and an induction target for the general case.

## Conjecture 5 — Tail concentration / second-moment bound
The sequence `n ↦ P(n,q)` has bounded variation: `Σ_{n} |P(n+1,q) − P(n,q)| < ∞` for fixed `q`.

- The key insight is that the forward recurrence is a contraction in the discrete-derivative norm
  once `n > q`, because each new term is a `1/n`-weighted average of previously bounded values.
- Why now? With `P` confirmed to live in `[0,1]`, summable fluctuations is the natural next
  quantitative step toward the limit conjectures 1–2, and partial sums are directly computable from
  the existing `ℚ` evaluator.
